newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: World Bank starts talks with debt-ridden new Congo.
newsitem.headline: World Bank starts talks with debt-ridden new Congo.

text.p: The World Bank held its first talks on Monday with Laurent Kabila's new Congo government and said it hoped to help sort out the country's huge debt burden.
Finance Minister Mawapanga Mwana Nanga told a news conference after meeting the Bank delegation,"This country has inherited a very large (foreign) debt that is estimated at more than $14 billion.
"The debt had been accumulated over a period of 32 years. We have been in power for 30 days. We need enough time to work this out. There is a way of finding solutions."
He said separate commissions would work on domestic and foreign debt.
"We want to know how much we owe and to whom. We have asked the World Bank and the other Bretton Woods institutions to be patient," Mawapanga said.

"We hope that when the information is available, we'll sit down with the government and its creditors to try to help," Bank delegation leader Callisto Madavo, vice-president for Africa, told the news conference.
"We have had a very constructive meeting, one in which we have really come to listen to you, hear what your plans are and how we might best help."

Mobutu Sese Seko, who seized power in 1965 and ran the economy into the ground, fled into exile when he was ousted last month after a seven-month rebellion by Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo.
The Bank suspended structural adjustment loans to Zaire in 1990 and withdrew entirely from the country three years later. The IMF, which also quit, has yet to make contact with Kabila.
At the time loans were cut, Bank officials estimated that two thirds of the national budget was being spent on the presidency and other related political functions.
Further corruption and mismanagement saw the other third scarcely reaching the social sector it was destined for.
The Bank and IMF have been criticised by Mobutu's foes both at home and abroad for continuing to lend to the former Zaire long after the extent of mismanagement was exposed.
But so far there has been no sign from major creditors of a willingness to write off part of the vast foreign debt.
The Alliance has yet to spell out a concrete strategy of how they plan to redevelop the country, devastated not only by decades of misrule but also by the recent conflict.
They say, however, that they can finance internally the major projects already announced.
These include a promised renaissance in road-building involving up to 5,500 km (3,500 miles) of tarred road, and a petrol pipeline to cross Africa's third largest country.

For the moment, analysts consider these projects to be pipe dreams. However, outside help for redevelopment is on offer on a grand scale should the government persuade international opinion it has sensible policies, Bank officials say.
